title: AI-Powered Diet Plans needs a Clinical Reality Check
summary: Are you enrolled in an AI-powered diet programme or paying for a personalised nutrition plan? Tracking every meal, counting calories and following app-generated recommendations, but are they actually making you healthier? As digital nutrition platforms make...

contentHtml:
New Delhi: Are you taking pictures of every meal, logging your food intake, counting calories or following a diet plan generated by an app? Digital nutrition is increasingly making these activities part of everyday health management. But the bigger question is does tracking what you eat necessarily mean you are eating better?For digital nutrition platforms, getting users to download an app, record meals, interact with nutritionists and complete a paid programme is only the first step. The harder task is demonstrating that these interventions lead to healthier dietary habits, improved nutritional status and measurable clinical outcomes.

Advt

A person may diligently upload meal photographs everyday without seeing any meaningful improvement in their health. Someone enrolled in a diabetes management programme may complete every consultation, but what matters is whether their blood glucose and HbA1c levels improve and remain under control.As AI begins to analyse food intake and generate personalised dietary recommendations, questions around clinical supervision, accuracy, adherence and long-term effectiveness become more pressing.

The industry is yet to answer on a basic question are digital nutrition platforms helping people become healthier, or are they simply getting better at tracking what people eat?

Such questions are becoming increasingly important as digital healthcare companies expand their offerings beyond fitness and weight management into diabetes management, obesity and preventive healthcare. With artificial intelligence (AI) entering dietary assessment and personalised meal recommendations, the industry is also facing greater scrutiny over the quality, safety and clinical relevance of the advice being delivered.

The distinction between user engagement and health outcomes is particularly important, says Ashwin Bhadri, Founder and CEO, Equinox Labs."The industry needs to distinguish between activity and impact. An individual logging meals every day does not necessarily mean their nutritional health is improving. Engagement metrics tell us whether people are using a platform; however, they do not tell us whether they are eating better, correcting nutritional deficiencies, or improving their metabolic health," he says.

Advt

Bhadri argues that platforms need to move beyond app usage and examine indicators such as dietary diversity, nutritional adequacy, weight, waist circumference, blood glucose and other clinically relevant parameters.While Equinox Labs focuses on testing, food safety and compliance rather than operating digital nutrition programmes, Bhadri believes the industry's health claims must be supported by measurable evidence.

"If a platform claims to improve health, it must demonstrate that improvement through appropriate and measurable indicators," he says.Dr Gowri Kulkarni, Director of Doctor Relations and Head of Medical Operations, MediBuddy, makes a similar distinction between platform activity and actual progress.

Advt

She points out that regular meal uploads and calorie tracking may indicate participation, but the real measure is whether an individual's health parameters improve over time.For someone enrolled in a diabetes management programme, for instance, a reduction in HbA1c from 7.5 to 6.5 over three to six months would provide a more objective indication of progress than the number of consultations attended or meals logged."Ultimately, platforms need to look at the relationship between the engagement they see and the health outcomes that follow," she says.Clinical supervision cannot be an afterthought

The question of clinical accountability becomes more significant when digital nutrition services move into managing chronic conditions.Dietary advice for a generally healthy individual is different from recommendations for someone living with diabetes, obesity, nutritional deficiencies or multiple co-existing conditions. A standardised diet plan or an algorithm-generated recommendation may not adequately account for medical history, medication, allergies or individual nutritional requirements.Dr Kulkarni believes managing these conditions requires coordination between different specialists rather than isolated dietary interventions.A diabetologist, for instance, would monitor blood glucose and cholesterol levels, while a nutritionist would assess dietary habits and nutritional intake. Fitness professionals can help individuals establish exercise routines, while mental health professionals can address the behavioural and emotional challenges associated with managing chronic conditions."What matters is that these recommendations do not operate in isolation. There needs to be a clinical team overseeing the individual's progress, ensuring that the advice is appropriate to their health needs and that different interventions work together," she says.The growing use of AI adds another layer to this responsibility. While algorithms can analyse food intake and generate personalised recommendations, their usefulness depends on the quality and completeness of the information they receive.Bhadri cautions that a recommendation suitable for one individual may be inappropriate for another because of medical history, allergies, nutritional deficiencies, medication or co-existing conditions.India's dietary diversity also presents a practical challenge. A recommendation based on a standardised Western diet may have little relevance to someone whose everyday meals are built around regional Indian ingredients and preparations."AI should assist qualified nutritionists and healthcare professionals, not replace their judgement," he says.Doctors, he argues, must retain authority over medical diagnosis and treatment, while qualified nutrition professionals should oversee dietary interventions, particularly for individuals with existing health conditions. AI-generated recommendations also need validation and monitoring.When users drop out, the numbers can tell a different storyAdherence remains another major challenge for digital nutrition programmes. Initial enthusiasm does not always translate into sustained behavioural change.Work schedules, family responsibilities, food preferences and affordability can all influence whether users continue with a programme.Bhadri believes companies need to examine these reasons rather than simply classify people who stop using an app as inactive users."If a programme requires someone to completely change their lifestyle without considering their everyday realities, disengagement is almost inevitable," he says.Recommendations, he argues, must be practical, culturally relevant, affordable and adaptable to individual circumstances.He also raises a concern about how platforms calculate and communicate programme outcomes. A company reporting that 70 per cent of its users achieved a particular health improvement needs to clarify whether that figure represents everyone who enrolled or only those who completed the programme and returned for follow-up assessments.These are significantly different populations and can produce very different conclusions.Companies, he says, should disclose original enrolment numbers, follow-up participation, the number of users with available clinical measurements and the methodology used to calculate outcomes."Missing data should not simply disappear from the final report. Users who disengage are part of the programme population, and excluding them without explanation can create an overly favourable picture," he says.He recommends that platforms report both completion-based and overall enrolment-based outcomes, with appropriate statistical treatment of missing information.This is particularly relevant in a market where programme completion and weight-loss percentages can become important selling points.Eight weeks of progress does not establish lasting changeAnother weakness in the way digital nutrition programmes are evaluated is the emphasis on short intervention periods.An eight- or twelve-week programme may demonstrate initial improvements, but it does not establish whether users maintain those changes six or twelve months later.For Bhadri, the more meaningful test is what happens when intensive coaching, reminders and structured interventions are withdrawn."I believe digital nutrition platforms should build longer follow-up periods into their evaluation models. Six-month and twelve-month assessments can provide a much clearer picture of whether people have maintained their dietary changes and whether improvements in relevant health markers have continued," he says.Dr Kulkarni, however, points out that sustaining lifestyle changes can be difficult without continued guidance.Regular expert follow-ups help individuals remain accountable, review their progress and seek advice when they encounter difficulties. Digital reminders can complement this process by prompting users to upload laboratory reports, record meals, track exercise and monitor sleep patterns.The objective, she says, should be to make health monitoring and follow-through part of everyday life rather than an activity restricted to the duration of a paid programme.The two perspectives highlight an important distinction for the industry: continued support may help sustain behavioural change, but platforms must also establish whether users can maintain improvements independently and what happens to their health parameters over time.Is weight loss becoming too convenient a measure of success?The industry's reliance on weight loss as a primary indicator of nutritional improvement is also attracting scrutiny.Weight is easy to communicate and track, but it does not necessarily provide a complete picture of an individual's nutritional health.A person may lose weight while also losing muscle mass or developing nutritional deficiencies. Another individual may see little change on the weighing scale but improve dietary diversity, muscle strength and metabolic health."Weight loss has become an overly convenient measure of nutritional success. Weight is easy to communicate, easy to track, and easy to market. But nutritional health is considerably more complex," Bhadri says.He believes platforms need to incorporate a wider range of indicators, including body composition, micronutrient status, dietary diversity, metabolic parameters and physical function, depending on individual requirements.This is particularly relevant in India, where undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, obesity and metabolic disorders coexist. A calorie-deficit approach cannot address all these nutritional challenges.Dr Kulkarni also believes the focus needs to move beyond the weighing scale towards metabolic health, fat loss and visceral fat.The challenge for digital platforms is to help consumers understand that body weight alone does not establish whether someone is becoming healthier. Consistent health education, she says, can help shift this understanding.The evidence behind health claimsAs platforms increasingly position their services around diabetes management, obesity and metabolic health, the nature of their claims also needs closer examination.There is a difference between providing nutritional guidance and claiming to manage a medical condition. The latter requires a stronger evidence base.Bhadri believes significant health claims should be supported by appropriately designed clinical studies, validated outcome measures and, wherever possible, independent evaluation.He also argues that the results should be relevant to the population being served. Demonstrating weight loss over eight weeks, for instance, is not sufficient evidence to establish improvements in long-term metabolic health."The industry should be comfortable sharing the methodology, sample size, study duration, limitations, and actual results behind its claims," he says.For Dr Kulkarni, the credibility of digital health information is equally important. With social media already crowded with individual experiences, diet recommendations and wellness advice, digital healthcare platforms need to distinguish reliable, science-backed information from unverified claims.The emphasis, she says, should be on the credibility and practical usefulness of health information rather than the volume of content being delivered.From consumer subscriptions to mainstream healthcareThe question of clinical evidence is also likely to become more important as digital nutrition services enter employer wellness programmes and become part of wider healthcare offerings.Dr Kulkarni sees growing interest among younger employees in preventive healthcare benefits, extending beyond treatment when an illness occurs. Employers are increasingly recognising the need to identify health risks early and encourage healthier habits among their workforce.She points to chronic disease management programmes across MediBuddy's corporate engagements, where individuals' health parameters have shown improvements in subsequent annual health check-ups.Examples include individuals with prediabetes bringing blood sugar levels back to the normal range, people with diabetes achieving better-controlled HbA1c levels and those with elevated cholesterol or triglycerides recording improvements.However, the specific programme outcomes, participant numbers and magnitude of these improvements have not been quantified in the responses.For Bhadri, the integration of digital nutrition into mainstream healthcare will make evidence and accountability increasingly important. Hospitals, insurers and employers will need to understand whether interventions are appropriate for their populations, whether qualified professionals are involved and whether meaningful improvements can be demonstrated.Commercial viability, meanwhile, cannot come at the expense of clinical safeguards.Technology can reduce repetitive administrative work, improve monitoring and help professionals reach larger populations. But qualified professionals, appropriate clinical oversight, validated assessments and reliable testing cannot be treated as optional costs."There is a difference between making healthcare more affordable and making it cheaper by compromising the very safeguards that make it trustworthy," Bhadri says.He also emphasises the need to separate clinical decision-making from commercial targets, particularly when platforms recommend supplements, products or paid services. Recommendations must be based on an individual's nutritional requirements rather than sales objectives.Will the industry agree on common outcome standards?One of the larger gaps in digital nutrition is the absence of consistent definitions of success across platforms.Companies may report enrolments, programme completion, weight loss or improvements in clinical parameters using different measurement periods and methodologies. This makes it difficult for consumers, healthcare providers and potential institutional partners to compare the effectiveness of different interventions.Bhadri supports common outcome standards covering enrolment, completion rates, follow-up participation, clinical improvements and the duration for which those improvements are sustained.He also believes consumers should have access to information about the qualifications of professionals involved, the evidence supporting an intervention and its limitations."Transparency is not a threat to innovation. It is what builds confidence in innovation," he says.The larger question facing digital nutrition companies is no longer how many people they can bring onto a platform or how frequently users interact with it. It is whether the intervention makes a measurable difference to their health, whether that improvement can be independently verified and whether it lasts.As Bhadri puts it, "The real test is whether people are healthier after using the platform, whether those improvements can be measured reliably and whether they continue after the programme ends."For an industry built around helping people change how they eat and live, proving that change may ultimately matter more than demonstrating how many people downloaded an app.
